Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls you in the middle of the night, crying, because they just received some devastating family news.
Situation2: This morning is the voter’s only chance to grab a valid ID from home, though the polls remain open tomorrow.
Story:
My phone buzzed at 2 a.m., jolting me awake. It was Sam, sobbing so hard I could barely make out the words. His father had just been rushed to the hospital, and he needed someone to talk to. I sat up, heart pounding, listening as he poured out his fear and confusion. I knew he needed me to stay on the line, to be present, to reassure him that he wasn’t alone.

But as the minutes ticked by, my mind kept drifting to the morning ahead. Today was the only window I had to swing by my apartment and grab my ID—without it, I couldn’t vote tomorrow. The polls would still be open, but my work schedule was packed, and this was my one shot. I felt torn, guilt gnawing at me. Sam’s pain was raw and immediate, but so was my responsibility as a voter. I wanted to be the friend he needed, but the clock was ticking, and I couldn’t ignore the other promise I’d made to myself. My hands shook as I tried to comfort him, wrestling with the impossible choice looming over me.
